title: A regular conductor element identifies total fractions and normalization
statement:
Let $m\ge1$ be an integer. For $1\le i\le m$, let $D_i$ be a commutative integral domain, let $E_i=\operatorname{Frac}(D_i)$ be its field of fractions, and suppose every element of $E_i$ satisfying a monic polynomial with coefficients in $D_i$ belongs to $D_i$. Put $B=\prod_{i=1}^mD_i$, let $A\subseteq B$ be a unital subring (a subset containing $0,1$ and closed under addition, negation and multiplication), and suppose there is $t\in A$ such that multiplication by $t$ is injective on $B$ and $tB\subseteq A$. A non-zero-divisor on a ring $C$ means an element $s$ such that multiplication by $s$ is injective; write $Q(C)$ for the localization of $C$ at all its non-zero-divisors [def-weil-pbc-module-localization, with $M=C$]. Ring maps use [def-weil-pbc-algebra-hom-quotient], and integrality and integral closure use [def-weil-pbc-integral-closure].
Every non-zero-divisor of $A$ remains a non-zero-divisor on $B$ and has nonzero image in each $D_i$. The formula
$$\iota:Q(A)\longrightarrow\prod_iE_i,\qquad r/s\longmapsto(r_i/s_i)_i$$
defines an injective ring map. There is a unique injective ring map
$$k:B\longrightarrow Q(A),\qquad k(b)=(tb)/t,$$
extending the localization map of $A$, and $\iota(k(b))=(b_i)_i$. For every non-zero-divisor $s\in B$, the element $ts\in A$ is a non-zero-divisor of $A$ and $k(s)^{-1}=t/(ts)$. The inclusion $A\subseteq B$ therefore induces an isomorphism $Q(A)\cong Q(B)$ whose restriction on $k(B)$ is the localization map of $B$.
Every $w\in Q(A)$ integral over $A$ lies in $k(B)$. Consequently, if every element of $B$ is integral over $A$, then
$$\operatorname{integralClosure}_{Q(A)}(A)=k(B).$$
All maps in these conclusions use the given inclusion $A\subseteq B$.

proof.text: In $B$, multiplication by $u=(u_i)$ is injective exactly when every $u_i\ne0$: if all coordinates are nonzero, $u_ib_i=0$ forces $b_i=0$ in each domain; if $u_i=0$, the nonzero vector $e_i$ with coordinate $1$ at $i$ and $0$ elsewhere is killed. Products of non-zero-divisors are non-zero-divisors, since a composite of injective multiplication maps is injective. In particular every $t_i\ne0$, and $t$ is also a non-zero-divisor on its subring $A$.

source.place: Tag 0C4A (lemma-2-branches-delta-1), proof of (1) implies (2), Cases I and II: explicit agent-supplied regular-conductor calculation; fraction arithmetic from Algebra Section 00CM (section-localization).

proof.text: Let $s$ be a non-zero-divisor of $A$ and suppose $sb=0$ in $B$. Since $tb\in A$, we have $s(tb)=0$ in $A$, hence $tb=0$, and injectivity of multiplication by $t$ on $B$ gives $b=0$. Thus $s$ is regular on $B$, and step 1 implies $s_i\ne0$ for every $i$. This proves the first assertion without assuming that any coordinate projection $A\to D_i$ is injective.

source.place: Tag 0C4A (lemma-2-branches-delta-1), proof of (1) implies (2), Cases I and II: explicit agent-supplied regular-conductor calculation; fraction arithmetic from Algebra Section 00CM (section-localization).

proof.text: Apply the fraction construction of [def-weil-pbc-module-localization] to $C=A$ and $C=B$, with $S$ the non-zero-divisors. Its relation simplifies to $r/s=r^{\prime}/s^{\prime}$ if and only if $s^{\prime}r=sr^{\prime}$, because the extra factor in $S$ is cancellable. By steps 1–2, this is equivalent to equality of all $r_i/s_i$ and $r_i^{\prime}/s_i^{\prime}$ in $E_i$. The displayed fraction addition and multiplication formulas therefore give injective unital ring maps $\iota:Q(A)\to\prod_iE_i$ and $J:Q(B)\to\prod_iE_i$. In particular the localization maps of $A$ and $B$ are injective.

source.place: Tag 0C4A (lemma-2-branches-delta-1), proof of (1) implies (2), Cases I and II: explicit agent-supplied regular-conductor calculation; fraction arithmetic from Algebra Section 00CM (section-localization).

proof.text: Define $k(b)=(tb)/t$; the numerator belongs to $A$ by the conductor hypothesis and the denominator is regular by step 1. Coordinate cancellation gives $\iota(k(b))=(b_i)_i$. Hence $k$ is injective, and applying the injective map $\iota$ to the addition, multiplication and unit identities proves that $k$ is a unital ring map. For $a\in A$, the fraction relation of [def-weil-pbc-module-localization] gives $(ta)/t=a/1$, so $k$ extends the localization map.

source.place: Tag 0C4A (lemma-2-branches-delta-1), proof of (1) implies (2), Cases I and II: explicit agent-supplied regular-conductor calculation; fraction arithmetic from Algebra Section 00CM (section-localization).

proof.text: If $h:B\to Q(A)$ is any unital ring map extending the localization map of $A$, then $h(t)h(b)=h(tb)=(tb)/1$. The element $h(t)=t/1$ has inverse $1/t$ in $Q(A)$ by the fraction formulas of [def-weil-pbc-module-localization]. Multiplying gives $h(b)=(tb)/t=k(b)$ for every $b$. This proves the claimed uniqueness even without imposing injectivity on $h$.

source.place: Tag 0C4A (lemma-2-branches-delta-1), proof of (1) implies (2), Cases I and II: explicit agent-supplied regular-conductor calculation; fraction arithmetic from Algebra Section 00CM (section-localization).

proof.text: For regular $u\in B$, the element $tu$ lies in $A$ and is regular on $B$ by step 1, hence on $A$. Thus $t/(tu)$ is a valid fraction in $Q(A)$. The fraction multiplication formula of [def-weil-pbc-module-localization] gives $k(u)\,t/(tu)=((tu)t)/(t(tu))=1$. Commutativity gives the other inverse identity, proving the asserted formula $k(u)^{-1}=t/(tu)$.

source.place: Tag 0C4A (lemma-2-branches-delta-1), proof of (1) implies (2), Cases I and II: explicit agent-supplied regular-conductor calculation; fraction arithmetic from Algebra Section 00CM (section-localization).

proof.text: The inclusion induces $F:Q(A)\to Q(B)$ by $r/s\mapsto r/s$: steps 1–2 make its denominators valid, and the relation and operation formulas of [def-weil-pbc-module-localization] make it a unital ring map. It satisfies $JF=\iota$. In the other direction put $H(b/u)=(tb)/(tu)$ for regular $u\in B$. Both numerator and denominator belong to $A$, and the latter is regular by step 6. If $b/u=b^{\prime}/u^{\prime}$, then $bu^{\prime}=b^{\prime}u$ in $B$, so $(tb)(tu^{\prime})=(tb^{\prime})(tu)$ in $A$. Thus $H$ is well-defined.

source.place: Tag 0C4A (lemma-2-branches-delta-1), proof of (1) implies (2), Cases I and II: explicit agent-supplied regular-conductor calculation; fraction arithmetic from Algebra Section 00CM (section-localization).

proof.text: For every $b/u\in Q(B)$, cancellation in each field gives $\iota(H(b/u))=(b_i/u_i)_i=J(b/u)$. Applying the injective $\iota$ and the ring map $J$ to the three ring-operation identities proves that $H$ is a unital ring map. Now $\iota HF=JF=\iota$ and $JFH=\iota H=J$; injectivity yields $HF=1$ and $FH=1$. Finally $F(k(b))=(tb)/t=b/1$ in $Q(B)$ by the fraction relation of [def-weil-pbc-module-localization]. The resulting isomorphism therefore has exactly the required compatibility with $B$.

source.place: Tag 0C4A (lemma-2-branches-delta-1), proof of (1) implies (2), Cases I and II: explicit agent-supplied regular-conductor calculation; fraction arithmetic from Algebra Section 00CM (section-localization).

proof.text: Let $w\in Q(A)$ be integral over $A$. By [def-weil-pbc-integral-closure] it satisfies $w^n+\sum_{j<n}a_jw^j=0$ with $n\ge1$ and $a_j\in A$. Write $z_i=\iota(w)_i$. Applying the ring map $\iota$ and then the $i$th projection gives $z_i^n+\sum_{j<n}(a_j)_iz_i^j=0$. The coefficients lie in $D_i$, so the stated hypothesis on $D_i$ gives $z_i\in D_i$. Thus $b=(z_i)_i\in B$ and $\iota(w)=\iota(k(b))$; injectivity gives $w=k(b)$. Conversely, if every $b\in B$ is integral over $A$, applying the ring map $k$ to its monic equation gives a monic equation for $k(b)$ with the same coefficients in $A$, since $k(a)=a/1$. The definition of integral closure then gives exactly the asserted equality.
